references.text: The immediate context: the guards who were holding Jesus mocked and beat him ([ref:Luk 22:63-64|Luke 22:63-64]). Verse 65 summarizes that they also said many other mocking and blasphemous things against him.
Matthew's parallel account of how Jesus was mocked, spat on, and beaten during the trial before the high priest ([ref:Matt 26:67-68|Matthew 26:67-68]).
Mark's parallel account where some began to spit on Jesus, cover his face, and beat him ([ref:Mark 14:65|Mark 14:65]).

Jesus speaks about blasphemy – here in Luke 22:65 it is he himself who is subjected to blasphemous speech, which stands in sharp contrast to the accusations of blasphemy directed against him ([ref:Matt 12:31-32|Matthew 12:31-32]).

Isaiah's prophecy about the suffering servant who was despised and rejected by men ([ref:Jes 53:3|Isaiah 53:3]). The mockery and blasphemous words against Jesus fulfill this prophecy that the Messiah would be despised.

The psalmist's lament: "All who see me mock me, they curl their lips and shake their heads" ([ref:Sal 22:7-8|Psalm 22:7-8]). This messianic psalm foretells the scorn and mockery that the Messiah would endure.
The psalmist describes being made an object of slander and mockery ([ref:Sal 69:10|Psalm 69:10]). This psalm was understood in a messianic sense and points to the suffering Jesus endured.

Peter writes that Christ, when he was reviled, did not revile in return, and when he suffered, he made no threats ([ref:1 Pet 2:23|1 Peter 2:23]). This shows Jesus' response to the blasphemous speech directed at him.

The mockery of Jesus also continued at the cross, where both the council members and the soldiers ridiculed him ([ref:Luk 23:35-36|Luke 23:35-36]), showing a pattern of persistent blasphemous speech against Jesus.
